## Learning Objectives

By the end of today's session, you should be able to:

- understand how Quarto connects **text, code, and results**
- use Markdown, code chunks, and YAML to structure reproducible documents
- generate and customize figures, tables, citations, and outputs
- recognize how Quarto supports reproducible research communication

::: notes
Key teaching goal: Communication and reproducibility, not memorization of syntax.

Participants do not need to memorize every option or command. The goal is understanding the workflow and knowing where to find additional tools when needed.

Emphasize:

Write → Analyze → Render → Communicate
:::


## Communicate

**R4DS Chapters 28-29**

::: notes

R4DS argues that communication is an essential part of the data science workflow.

Data science is not:

Data → Analysis → Done

Instead:

Data → Analysis → Communication → Impact

The goal of this section is not learning how to communicate ideas effectively. That comes from practice and experience.

Instead, we are focusing on the technical tools that allow us to communicate our analyses reproducibly.

Ask:

- How many of you have copied a figure from R into PowerPoint?
- How many have copied a table into Word?
- How many have had to recreate a figure months later?
- How many have struggled to remember how a result was generated?

Quarto helps address these problems by keeping the analysis and communication connected.

Key question:

"If nobody can understand or reproduce your work, did the analysis accomplish its goal?"
:::


# Chapter 28: Quarto

## Basics

**What is Quarto?**
A publishing system for creating reproducible documents by combining code, text, and visualizations.

**Every Quarto document contains four building blocks:**

- **YAML** – document settings (title, author, output)
- **Markdown** – narrative text
- **Code chunks** – R code that performs analyses
- **Rendered output** – tables, figures, and results

Example:

````markdown
```text
---
title: "Exercise Intervention Results"
author: "Morgan Brucks"
format: html
---

## Participant Characteristics

This report summarizes baseline demographics.
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
summary(demographics)
```
````



::: {.callout-note}
Think of Quarto as a recipe:

- YAML tells Quarto what to make.
- Markdown explains the steps to make the recipe.
- Code performs the steps or analysis.
- Rendering produces the finished meal or document.
:::


## Editors

Quarto provides two ways to edit your documents: the Visual Editor for a word processor-like experience and the Source Editor for writing directly in Markdown. Both produce the same final document, so you can choose the workflow that best fits your needs.

**Visual**
<img src="https://r4ds.hadley.nz/quarto/quarto-visual-editor.png"/>


**Source**

````markdown
## Text formatting

*italic* **bold** ~~strikeout~~ `code`

superscript^2^ subscript~2~

[underline]{.underline} [small caps]{.smallcaps}

## Headings

# 1st Level Header

## 2nd Level Header

### 3rd Level Header

## Lists

-   Bulleted list item 1

-   Item 2

    -   Item 2a

    -   Item 2b

1.  Numbered list item 1

2.  Item 2.
    The numbers are incremented automatically in the output.

## Links and images

<http://example.com>

[linked phrase](http://example.com)

![optional caption text](quarto.png){fig-alt="Quarto logo and the word quarto spelled in small case letters"}

## Tables

| First Header | Second Header |
|--------------|---------------|
| Content Cell | Content Cell  |
| Content Cell | Content Cell  |
````

## Markdown vs. HTML

Both Markdown and HTML can be used to format Quarto documents. **Markdown is the preferred syntax for most writing tasks because it is concise, readable, and easy to maintain.** HTML is available when you need additional formatting or customization.

| Feature | Markdown | HTML |
|:--------|:---------|:-----|
| **Bold** | `**text**` | `<strong>text</strong>` |
| **Italic** | `*text*` | `<em>text</em>` |
| **Heading** | `## Heading` | `<h2>Heading</h2>` |
| **Bullet List** | `- Item` | `<ul><li>Item</li></ul>` |
| **Numbered List** | `1. Item` | `<ol><li>Item</li></ol>` |
| **Link** | `[Posit](https://posit.co)` | `<a href="https://posit.co">Posit</a>` |
| **Image** | `![Logo](logo.png)` | `<img src="logo.png">` |



**Example: Custom HTML Styling**

```html
<span style="color:#0055A4; font-weight:bold;">
Important Result
</span>
```

Markdown cannot easily apply custom colors or styles, but HTML can.


::: {.callout-note title="Hadley's Philosophy"}

**Use Markdown for almost everything.** It is easier to read, write, and collaborate on.

Use **HTML only when you need formatting that Markdown doesn't support**, such as custom styling, colors, layouts, or embedded web content.

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Take-Home Message"}

You do **not** need to learn HTML to be productive in Quarto. Markdown covers the vast majority of everyday writing tasks, while HTML is there when you need more control over the appearance of your document.

:::

## Code Chunks

Code chunks execute your analysis and insert the results directly into your document. Chunk labels and options help organize your work while controlling what appears in the final output.

### Chunk Labels

Give chunks meaningful names so they are easier to identify, troubleshoot, and reference.

```text
#| label: participant-demographics
```

### Chunk Options

Chunk options control **what your audience sees**, not what your code does.

| Option | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `echo: false` | Hide code, show output |
| `eval: false` | Show code, don't run it |
| `warning: false` | Hide warnings |
| `message: false` | Hide package startup messages |

::: {.callout-tip}
**Remember:**

- **`echo`** controls whether the **code is displayed**.
- **`eval`** controls whether the **code is executed**.

These options can be combined. For example, `echo: true` with `eval: false` displays the code without running it, while `echo: false` with `eval: true` runs the code but only displays the results.
:::

### Global Options

Set default chunk behavior once using a setup chunk.

```r
#| label: setup
#| include: false

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE
)
```

::: {.callout-note}
**Chunk options** apply to a single chunk, while **global options** become the default for every chunk in your document.
:::

### Inline Code

Inline code inserts **individual values** directly into your narrative, helping keep reports accurate as your data change.

````markdown
The dataset contains `` `r nrow(mtcars)` `` observations.
````

::: notes
Inline code is one of Quarto's most useful features for research reporting.

Rather than manually typing values into your report, Quarto calculates them automatically every time the document is rendered.

This greatly reduces copy-and-paste errors and keeps text synchronized with tables and figures.

How many of you have ever updated a figure but forgotten to update the number in the paragraph above it?
Inline code solves exactly that problem.
:::


## Figures and Tables

Quarto automatically creates publication-ready figures and tables directly from your analysis. Update your code, render the document, and every result stays synchronized.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Display Code Only**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mpg, aes(class)) +
  geom_bar()
```

`eval: false` displays the code without running it.

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Display Figure**

```{r}
#| echo: false

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mpg, aes(class)) +
  geom_bar()
```

`echo: false` hides the code and displays only the figure.

:::

::::

**Tables in Quarto**

Quarto supports several table packages depending on your desired output. Here are two of the most commonly used.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

`gt`

**Source**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(gt)

mtcars |>
  head() |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = mpg,
    decimals = 1
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Vehicle Characteristics"
  )
```

**Output**

```{r}
#| echo: false

library(gt)

mtcars |>
  head() |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = mpg,
    decimals = 1
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Vehicle Characteristics"
  )
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

`flextable`

**Source**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(flextable)

mtcars |>
  head() |>
  flextable() |>
  colformat_num(
    j = "mpg",
    digits = 1
  ) |>
  autofit()
```

**Output**

```{r}
#| echo: false

library(flextable)

mtcars |>
  head() |>
  flextable() |>
  colformat_num(
    j = "mpg",
    digits = 1
  ) |>
  autofit()
```

:::

::::

::: {.callout-note}
**Choosing a table package**

- **`gt`** creates polished, publication-quality tables and works especially well for HTML reports.
- **`flextable`** is designed for Microsoft Word and PowerPoint, making it a great choice for collaborators and manuscripts.
:::

::: notes

Traditional workflow:

- Create figure
- Save figure
- Copy into Word or PowerPoint
- Repeat whenever the analysis changes

Quarto workflow:

- Update code
- Render document
- Every figure and table updates automatically

Point out that **gt** excels for HTML reports and websites, while **flextable** integrates especially well with Word and PowerPoint.

:::

## YAML: Configuring Your Document

YAML is the header section of a Quarto document that provides instructions for how your document should be created and formatted.

Think of YAML as the **configuration file** for your document.

YAML can:

- define document information
- customize appearance
- add extensions and functionality
- control formatting behavior

Example:

```yaml
---
title: "Exercise Intervention Results"
author: "Morgan Brucks"
format: html
---
```

::: {.callout-note}
YAML is processed before your R code runs. It tells Quarto how to build your final document.
:::

::: notes
If Markdown is the content of your document and R code is the analysis, YAML is the instruction manual telling Quarto how to assemble everything.
:::

## Extending and Styling Quarto

Quarto provides multiple ways to customize your documents beyond the default settings.

| Tool | Purpose | Example Uses |
|------|---------|--------------|
| **Quarto extensions** | Add reusable functionality | templates, themes, publishing workflows |
| **CSS** | Customize HTML appearance | colors, fonts, spacing, layouts |
| **SCSS** | Build advanced CSS styles | reusable style systems |
| **Lua filters** | Modify document behavior | custom formatting rules |
| **LaTeX** | Customize PDF output | manuscript formatting |

::: {.callout-tip}
Most users will customize Quarto through YAML, themes, and CSS. Advanced tools like Lua filters and LaTeX provide additional control when needed.
:::

## Example: Styling with YAML

YAML can connect your document to themes, stylesheets, and other custom resources.

```yaml
format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
    css: styles.css
```

This allows you to customize:

- fonts
- colors
- spacing
- page appearance
- document branding

::: notes
You can think of these tools as different levels of customization. YAML tells Quarto what you want. CSS changes how HTML looks. LaTeX controls PDF styling. Lua filters are for more advanced document transformations.
:::

## Citations in Quarto

Quarto can automatically manage citations and references using a bibliography file.

The bibliography is connected through the YAML header:

```yaml
---
title: "Exercise Intervention Results"
author: "Morgan Brucks"
format: html
bibliography: references.bib
csl: https://www.zotero.org/styles/apa
---
```

::: notes
The YAML header tells Quarto where to find citation information and which citation style to use.

Here we are using APA formatting, which is common in behavioral science and health research.
:::

**Adding Citations**

Citations are added directly within the text using the author-year citation key.

Example:

```markdown
Regular physical activity is associated with improved health outcomes 
[@piercy2018].
```

Quarto automatically formats the citation:

> Regular physical activity is associated with improved health outcomes (Piercy et al., 2018).


**Reference List**

At the end of the document, Quarto automatically generates:

```markdown
## References
```

from the entries stored in:

```
references.bib
```

::: {.callout-note}
References are stored separately from the document content, making citations reusable and automatically updated across projects.
:::

::: notes
Quarto separates the writing from the references. The .qmd contains the narrative, the .bib file contains citation information, and the YAML header tells Quarto how to format everything.
:::

## Troubleshooting Quarto

Most Quarto errors come from three places:

| Error Type | Common Causes | Where to Check |
|------------|---------------|----------------|
| **R code** | Missing package, object not found, syntax errors | Code chunk |
| **Quarto/YAML** | Incorrect indentation, missing `:`, invalid options | YAML header |
| **Markdown** | Unclosed chunks, missing brackets, formatting issues | Document text |

**Common Errors**

- package not installed or loaded
- object does not exist
- YAML indentation errors
- missing parentheses or quotation marks
- unclosed code chunks

::: {.callout-tip}
**Debugging workflow**

1. Read the error message  
2. Find the line where the error occurred  
3. Identify whether it is R, YAML, or Markdown  
4. Fix one issue at a time  
5. Render again
:::

**Example: Object Not Found**

Error:

```text
object 'demographics' not found
```

Possible causes:

```r
summary(demographics)
```

- Dataset was never loaded
- Dataset name is misspelled
- Code chunk creating the object did not run

::: notes
The most important troubleshooting skill is learning to classify the error. If the message mentions YAML, look at the header. If it says could not find function, think package. If it says object not found, think about whether the object exists and whether the previous code ran.
Rendering is not just creating the final document. It is also a test that your workflow can be reproduced from start to finish.
A successful render is a reproducibility check. Render early and often.
:::

## Chapter 28 Summary: Quarto

Quarto combines **text, code, and results** into reproducible documents.

**Key Concepts**

| Concept | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| **Quarto documents** | Combine narrative, analysis, and outputs in one place |
| **Markdown** | Create readable, structured documents using simple syntax |
| **Code chunks** | Execute R code and insert results automatically |
| **Chunk options** | Control what code and output appear |
| **Figures & tables** | Generate reproducible, publication-ready outputs |
| **YAML** | Configure document settings and customization |
| **Citations** | Manage references automatically through bibliography files |

::: {.callout-tip}
**The Quarto workflow**

Write → Analyze → Render → Communicate

When your data or code change, your document updates with them.
:::

::: notes
Key message:

Quarto is not just a way to make pretty documents. It creates a reproducible connection between:

- the code you write
- the analysis you perform
- the results you communicate

Review:

1. Documents are structured using Markdown and YAML.
2. Code chunks allow analysis and communication to happen together.
3. Chunk options control what the audience sees.
4. Figures and tables update automatically when code changes.
5. Citations and references can be managed reproducibly.

Transition:

The important idea from Chapter 28 is not memorizing YAML options or chunk syntax. The important idea is that Quarto creates a reproducible pipeline from analysis to communication.
Now that we understand how Quarto documents are created and customized, Chapter 29 focuses on the different formats we can create from the same source document.
::: 

# Chapter 29: Quarto Formats

## Chapter 29: Quarto Formats

One Quarto document can be transformed into multiple output formats.

The content and analysis stay the same, while the final product changes based on the audience and purpose.

::: {.callout-note}
**One source → many outputs**
:::

| Format | Best For | Example Uses |
|--------|----------|--------------|
| **HTML** | Interactive web documents | Reports, dashboards, online supplements |
| **PDF** | Fixed-layout documents | Manuscripts, formal reports |
| **DOCX** | Editable documents | Collaborator drafts, reviews |
| **Revealjs** | HTML presentations | Research talks, workshops |
| **PPTX** | PowerPoint slides | Meetings, presentations |

::: notes
The important concept is that we are not recreating the same information in multiple programs.

Instead:

Same analysis + same narrative + different output format.

For example:

- A researcher could create an HTML report for collaborators.
- A PDF version for documentation.
- A presentation version for a conference.

All from the same Quarto source file.
:::

## Changing Formats with YAML

The output format is controlled in the YAML header.

HTML:

```yaml
format: html
```

PDF:

```yaml
format: pdf
```

Word:

```yaml
format: docx
```

Presentation:

```yaml
format: revealjs
```

The analysis and narrative remain the same. Only the output changes.

## Interactivity with Shiny

Quarto can also create interactive applications using Shiny.

Instead of a static report:

```
Data → Analysis → Report
```

Interactive workflows allow:

```
Data → Analysis → User Exploration
```

Examples:

- interactive dashboards
- data exploration tools
- decision-support tools
- participant tracking systems

::: {.callout-tip}
Shiny allows users to interact with results without needing to write R code.
:::

::: notes

Example:

A static figure shows intervention outcomes.

A Shiny application could allow a user to:

- select a participant group
- adjust variables
- explore trends
- filter results

The researcher builds the tool; the end user interacts with the results.

:::

## Chapter 29 Summary: Formats

Quarto allows researchers to communicate the same work in different ways.

**One Source → Many Outputs**

A single `.qmd` file can become:

- research reports
- manuscripts
- presentations
- interactive dashboards
- collaborator documents

::: {.callout-note}
The goal is not creating more documents.

The goal is creating **one reproducible source that can be shared in many formats.**
:::

::: notes
Highlight Brian's Disclosure report
A disclosure report is not just a PDF. It is a reproducible report where the data, analysis, figures, tables, and formatting are all connected. If the data update, the report can update.
Give an example of a use case for my lab.
Ask: What other use cases can you think of?
:::

## Best Practices for Quarto

A reproducible workflow requires more than code.

✓ Render often  
✓ Keep files organized  
✓ Write narrative alongside analysis  
✓ Document decisions  
✓ Use meaningful chunk labels  
✓ Save source files with projects  
✓ Embrace reproducibility


## Wrap-Up: Key Takeaways

**Chapter 28: Quarto**

Quarto brings together:

- **Narrative** → explain your work using Markdown
- **Code** → integrate analysis directly into documents
- **Results** → automatically generate figures and tables
- **Configuration** → customize documents through YAML
- **Citations** → manage references reproducibly

**Key idea:**

> A Quarto document connects the analysis process with the final communication product.

**Chapter 29: Quarto Formats**

Quarto allows one source document to become many outputs:

- reports
- manuscripts
- presentations
- Word documents
- interactive applications

**Key idea:**

> Write once. Render many ways.

::: {.callout-tip}
Quarto is not just a document creation tool. It is a reproducible workflow for communicating research.
:::
